sentences.text: December 7, 1941.
A date that would change the course of history.
Shortly before eight o'clock on a quiet Sunday morning, the first Japanese aircraft appeared over Oahu.
Within two hours, much of the United States Pacific Fleet lay burning in Pearl Harbor.
More than two thousand four hundred Americans were dead.
It was one of the most daring naval operations ever attempted, and one of the most consequential mistakes in modern history.
To understand how it happened, we have to go back ten years, and thousands of miles to the west.
In 1931, Japan's army seized Manchuria.
Six years later, fighting near Beijing escalated into full-scale war with China.
Japan's leaders sought an empire that could supply what the home islands lacked: iron, rubber, and above all, oil.
Japan imported most of its oil, the bulk of it from the United States.
In 1940, Japanese forces moved into northern French Indochina, and Japan signed the Tripartite Pact with Germany and Italy.
Washington answered with economic pressure, restricting exports of scrap iron and aviation fuel.
In July 1941, Japanese troops entered southern Indochina.
The United States froze Japanese assets, and American oil exports to Japan stopped. Britain and the Dutch government in exile followed.
Tokyo faced a choice: give up its conquests in China, or seize the oil fields of the Dutch East Indies by force.
And on the flank of any move south lay the United States Pacific Fleet, based since 1940 at Pearl Harbor.
Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, commander of Japan's Combined Fleet, had studied at Harvard and served as naval attaché in Washington.
He knew America's industrial strength, and he opposed war with the United States.
But if war came, he believed Japan's only chance was to strike first: cripple the Pacific Fleet at the outset, and buy time to seize the resources of Southeast Asia.
In November 1940, British carrier aircraft had crippled the Italian fleet at anchor in Taranto.
The lesson was clear: a fleet in harbor was vulnerable from the air.
Yamamoto was not the plan's only author.
Air staff officer Minoru Genda worked out much of the operational detail, Yamamoto's own staff refined it, and the Naval General Staff approved it only after Yamamoto threatened to resign.
Pearl Harbor was shallow, only about forty feet deep, too shallow for ordinary aerial torpedoes.
Japanese engineers fitted wooden fins to their torpedoes, and aircrews trained for months over Kagoshima Bay.
American cryptanalysts had broken Japan's top diplomatic cipher, known to them as Purple.
The decrypts, code-named MAGIC, let Washington read Tokyo's diplomatic messages, often within hours.
But MAGIC was diplomatic traffic. Japan's main naval code was not being read in time, and the strike force sailed under strict radio silence.
In September 1941, Tokyo asked its consulate in Honolulu to report the berths of warships in Pearl Harbor, using a grid of five areas.
Washington decoded the message in October. It was one of many requests for information about American bases, and its significance was missed.
On November 27, Navy commanders in the Pacific received a message that began: "This dispatch is to be considered a war warning."
It pointed to likely Japanese moves against the Philippines, Thailand, or Borneo. It did not name Hawaii.
On the night of December 6, Washington decoded the first thirteen parts of a long Japanese reply.
The final part arrived the next morning, with an instruction to deliver it at precisely one p.m. Washington time, seven thirty in Hawaii.
A warning from General George Marshall went by commercial telegraph. It reached the Army commander in Hawaii only after the attack.
That morning, two more warnings came and went.
At about a quarter to seven, the destroyer U.S.S. Ward fired on a midget submarine near the harbor entrance and sank it. Her report moved slowly up the chain of command.
At 7:02, at the Opana radar station, Privates Joseph Lockard and George Elliott detected a large formation about 132 miles to the north.
The duty officer, Lieutenant Kermit Tyler, believed it was a flight of B-17 bombers expected from California. The warning went no further.
The strike force, the Kido Butai, was commanded by Vice Admiral Chuichi Nagumo.
At its heart were six aircraft carriers: Akagi, Kaga, Soryu, Hiryu, Shokaku, and Zuikaku.
They were escorted by two battleships, two heavy cruisers, a light cruiser, and nine destroyers, with submarines scouting ahead and tankers to refuel at sea.
On November 26, the force left Hitokappu Bay in the Kuril Islands and steered east across the empty northern Pacific, far from shipping lanes, in winter seas.
On December 2, the fleet received the coded signal confirming the attack: "Climb Mount Niitaka."
Before dawn on December 7, some 230 miles north of Oahu, the carriers turned into the wind.
At six a.m., the first wave began to launch: one hundred eighty-three aircraft, torpedo bombers, level bombers, dive bombers, and Zero fighters.
The air attack was led by Commander Mitsuo Fuchida.
Over Oahu the formation divided.
Dive bombers and fighters struck the airfields, Wheeler, Hickam, Ford Island, and Kaneohe, where American planes stood parked wingtip to wingtip as a precaution against sabotage.
At 7:53, Fuchida radioed the signal that surprise had been achieved: "Tora! Tora! Tora!"
Seven battleships lay moored along Battleship Row, beside Ford Island. An eighth, Pennsylvania, sat in dry dock.
Torpedo bombers came in low across the harbor.
Oklahoma was hit by several torpedoes and capsized within minutes. West Virginia sank upright at her moorings.
Shortly after eight o'clock, an armor-piercing bomb struck U.S.S. Arizona and detonated her forward ammunition magazine.
The explosion tore the ship apart. One thousand one hundred seventy-seven of her crew were killed, nearly half of all Americans who died that day.
At about 8:55, a second wave of one hundred sixty-seven aircraft arrived. Surprise was gone, and they met heavy anti-aircraft fire.
Nevada, the only battleship to get underway, was bombed as she moved down the channel, and was beached to keep the harbor entrance clear.
By ten o'clock, the attackers were flying back to their carriers. Nagumo chose not to launch another strike.
The fuel tanks, repair shops, and submarine base were left largely intact. And the Pacific Fleet's aircraft carriers had not been in port.
In less than two hours, two thousand four hundred and three Americans were killed, sixty-eight of them civilians, and one thousand one hundred seventy-eight were wounded.
Eight battleships were damaged, four of them sunk. More than one hundred eighty aircraft were destroyed.
Aboard West Virginia, Mess Attendant Second Class Doris "Dorie" Miller helped carry his mortally wounded captain, Mervyn Bennion, to shelter.
Then he manned an anti-aircraft machine gun he had not been trained to use. Miller became the first African American to receive the Navy Cross. Captain Bennion was awarded the Medal of Honor.
At Kaneohe, Chief Aviation Ordnanceman John Finn fired a machine gun from an exposed position through the attack, despite multiple wounds. He, too, received the Medal of Honor.
Inside the capsized Oklahoma, men were trapped in the dark.
Civilian navy yard workers, organized by Julio DeCastro, cut through the hull for more than a day. They brought out thirty-two sailors alive.
Japan lost twenty-nine aircraft and five midget submarines. Sixty-four Japanese servicemen were killed. One submariner, Ensign Kazuo Sakamaki, was captured, the first Japanese prisoner of the war.
Over Kaneohe, Lieutenant Fusata Iida's fighter was hit and leaking fuel. He turned back toward the air station and crashed there. A marker stands at the site today.
The next day, President Franklin D. Roosevelt addressed a joint session of Congress.
"Yesterday, December 7th, 1941, a date which will live in infamy, the United States of America was suddenly and deliberately attacked by naval and air forces of the Empire of Japan."
Within the hour, Congress declared war on Japan: eighty-two to nothing in the Senate, three hundred eighty-eight to one in the House.
On December 11, Germany and Italy declared war on the United States.
The attack united a divided nation. Recruiting stations filled. Factories that had built cars turned to tanks, engines, and aircraft.
At Pearl Harbor, salvage crews raised and repaired most of the damaged ships. West Virginia, sunk at her moorings, would return to fight.
And American shipyards launched dozens of new aircraft carriers, large and small.
Tactically, Pearl Harbor was a stunning Japanese success. Strategically, it was a catastrophe.
The battleships it targeted were losing their central place in naval warfare. The carriers it missed, the base it left working, and the industrial power it provoked would decide the war.
Six months later, at Midway, American aviators sank four of the six carriers that had attacked Pearl Harbor: Akagi, Kaga, Soryu, and Hiryu.
A famous line has Yamamoto lamenting that Japan had awakened a sleeping giant. There is no evidence he ever said it. The words come from a 1970 film.
But the history they describe is real.
On September 2, 1945, Japan signed the instrument of surrender aboard U.S.S. Missouri in Tokyo Bay.
Among the American ships present was West Virginia, raised from the mud of Pearl Harbor.
Today, the wreck of U.S.S. Arizona still rests in Pearl Harbor, with more than nine hundred of her crew entombed inside.
A white memorial spans the hull, honoring the men who died on a Sunday morning that changed the course of history.
